notes: Workers are Python threads in one process; run inside the compose network (docker compose --profile bench run crucible).
claim = claim_next_task, heartbeat, complete are timed separately; each cycle is claim -> heartbeat -> complete.
B2's claims are B1's SQLite claims (hybrid), so only its recall is measured separately.
P-mcp adds a Step and a ToolCall write to every call, as the MCP server does.

B0/B1/B2 are embedded libraries running inside the crucible container (they have no server); the Plexus arms talk to the FalkorDB container over the compose network. B1/B2 use SQLite's built-in busy handler, which has no fairness queue, so tail latency under write contention is large; cross-process writers cannot be queued in-process.
recall includes embedding the query with the local bge-small model (one model instance per process, calls serialised by its lock) for B2, P and P-mcp.

honesty: Synthetic workloads and data only; one scenario family, a single-node database, scripted (non-LLM) workers.

L1 workers are threads sharing one backend object (each with its own DB connection / file descriptors); only C2's victims are separate OS processes killed with SIGKILL. Concurrency is real but not deterministic: seeds fix the workload (priorities, DAG shape, values, query times), not the interleaving.
Violations are reported as exact counts summed over all runs, never averaged.

B0 and B1 are configured competently (locks / transactions). Where they match Plexus the table says so; Plexus's advantage is claimed only for what a graph does better: provenance, dependency traversal, time travel, contradictions at write time and cascading forget.
L4 client latency is measured by Python threads in one process: at high worker counts it includes GIL queuing. Server-side run_time_ms is shown next to it for the Plexus arms.

C5 probes each arm's tool API and, for Plexus, the MCP runtime's tenant binding (a header cannot rebind a connection). It does not probe the HTTP View API: that API is read-only, names the tenant in the URL and has no authentication in v1, so isolation there is by deployment. For B0/B1/B2 nothing stops a process with file access from opening another tenant's directory, and Plexus does not enforce per-graph access control inside FalkorDB either; a client with database access can query any graph.
BASELINE §1 asks for one container per arm. B0/B1/B2 are embedded libraries with no server, so they run inside the crucible container; only FalkorDB (the Plexus arms) is a separate container.
Numbers from `--quick` runs, or from outside Docker (Windows port forward adds ~10 ms per round trip), are not the published figures.

L2: exact-match accuracy over a script-derived question set (43 questions, 10 families), one scenario, one model, one run per question; no LLM judge anywhere. Ground truth is computed from the scenario script, not read back from any arm.

Baselines are the same unmodified `claude -p` with no tools, shown their own artifacts at the same 32,000-character cap. At this scenario size the B0 and B1 artifacts fit in the cap without truncation, so the cap is not what limits them; B2 deliberately sees only its top-12 retrieved chunks.

Result in plain words: at this scenario size (12 tasks, 9 facts, 6 decisions) the whole B0 run is about 25k characters and the whole B1 dump about 18k, so Sonnet reads everything and answers every question; Plexus TIES them on accuracy. What Plexus does measurably better here is cost and determinism (no tokens, a few milliseconds, same answer every time versus 13-16k tokens and ~5 s per question). Whether accuracy diverges when the artifacts outgrow the context cap is NOT measured by this run.

Arm P answers each question with a hand-written Cypher statement per question family. That is the point of the comparison (a graph can answer these with one query) but it is also engineering effort the baselines do not get: the baselines were given no hand-written SQL or grep helpers either.

The Procedures family of BASELINE §2 is not in this set: the backend protocol has no procedure tool, so the arms cannot be compared on it. Cross-session recall is reduced to episodes recorded by agents (the protocol has no sessions).

The scenario is the P3 Acme script replayed on the backend protocol, plus three L2 additions (the forum-post poison fault, one extra builder decision, two project-scoped facts); see crucible/l2/scenario.py.

B1 and B2 (and B0's task file) keep only a task's final claimer, not the claim history; only B0's per-agent logs and Plexus's CLAIMED edges record who held an expired lease. Recovery questions therefore test what each arm's artifacts actually contain, as configured in L1.

L2-scale: exact-match accuracy over script-derived questions (40 generated, 10 families x 4; 36 asked after the pre-registered budget rule) about 20 independent sprints of one team history; one scenario family, one model (sonnet), one run per question; no LLM judge. Ground truth is computed from the per-sprint scenario ledgers, not read back from any arm. Pre-registered in docs/BASELINE.md before the first paid call.

The history is 20 repetitions of the same synthetic story with varied ids and values. Real histories are messier; sprints here do not interact, which favours retrieval (a question names its sprint and a sprint's records share its tag).
Every question names exactly one sprint, so competent keyword retrieval can find a sprint's records. Questions that aggregate across sprints (the strongest case for a graph) are NOT in this set.

Baselines are the same unmodified `claude -p --model sonnet` with no tools at the same 32,000-character cap, shown BM25-ranked chunks/rows (B0, B1) or vector top-12 (B2) selected with the question text. The selectors were written once, before any paid call, and not tuned afterwards.

Arm P answers with hand-written Cypher per question family (the same operations as the 43-question L2 run, with the sprint scoping listed in the results); that engineering effort is part of what P costs and the baselines get no equivalent helper.
